name: Ben Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing philosophy, politics and economics. A normal week is a big lecture on political theory, a tutorial in a group of five where we get torn apart over an essay, and an economics problem set that always takes longer than I plan. I play rugby on Wednesdays and go to chapel on Sundays, which keeps me sane. Friday and Saturday nights I pull pints at the Crown, a pub near campus.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how does money work for you right now, between family, the part-time job and the course?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Dad is a dairy farmer, about 90 cows, and Mum does the school office two days a week. They put in about half toward my rent and fees, and the rest is my pub wages and a bit saved from summer work on the farm. I'm not poor, but I know what a milk price drop does to the dinner table at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here is the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected. I use these tools sometimes, for essay outlines, but they get things wrong and I've learned to check. In the pub, regulars like Dai (an old farmer) ask me if the robots are coming, and I'd tell him to worry about the milk price instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved but still anxious about the usual things. Dad's farm runs on thin margins, feed costs keep rising, and a bad year could cost us a field. If the dairy buyer drops the price again, I'd have to find extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my shifts at the Crown, work the whole summer on the farm, and keep to my degree. I'd also ask the careers office about solicitor apprenticeship routes, because I'd like to compare them with three years of lectures. I'd save about 25 a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly it's the farm and my degree and what comes after it, which would be the same any year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still be a pressure for you if AI turns out to be hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, but it isn't a straight line to anywhere. PPE is a good degree, but there are lots of us, and I'm not sure what employer will want a philosopher. I'd say I'm hoping it makes me a better thinker and a hard worker, and the rest follows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about your degree if the world carries on as it is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The milk price, mainly. Last year the milk price dropped by a few pence a litre and Dad skipped a holiday and put off buying a new tractor. That's real, and it's more likely than a robot arriving at the farm gate.

say: I'd tell Dai, an old farmer at the pub, to worry about the **milk price** instead of robots.
I'd say AI tools get things wrong and I've learned to **check** them.
think: Dad's farm runs on **thin margins**, and a bad year could cost us a field.
A philosophy degree isn't a straight line to any **employer**.
do: Keep my **shifts** at the Crown and work all summer on the farm.
Ask the careers office about solicitor **apprenticeship** routes.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly about the farm and what comes after the degree.

Save 25 a week for fees and farm emergencies
Work the whole summer on Dad's farm to cover labour

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of change, and we shouldn't panic. It's reasonable for businesses to use tools that make them better, but they should keep the people who've worked for them for years. I'd say that at the pub and in chapel group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my degree is more exposed than I'd like. Reading, writing, summarising and arguing are exactly what the tools do well. The people who survive will be the ones with practical skills, like a trade or a profession with a licence. That makes the solicitor route look better to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for a solicitor apprenticeship at a local firm, because they pay while you learn and the profession has rules. I'd keep the degree option open for a year. I'd also learn to use AI tools properly for research, because everyone will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not about the farm. About my future income, and whether I've chosen something that is going to shrink under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of the farm and of your studies would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm's paperwork: milk records, tax returns, feed orders. Dad hates the farm's paperwork and spends every Sunday evening on it. If a tool does it, that's good. The milking itself and the animals stay hands-on for a long while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad about trying new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say try it on the paperwork first, because that's low risk and saves time. He's cautious, like me, and he'll want to see it working at another farm, so I'd find one near us that's tried it.

say: I'd say businesses should use useful tools but keep the **people** who've worked for them for years.
I'd say it at the pub and in **chapel** group.
think: Reading, writing, summarising and arguing are what the tools do **well**, so my degree is exposed.
Practical skills and **licensed** professions look safer, which makes the solicitor route better.
do: Apply for a **solicitor apprenticeship** at a local firm and keep the degree option open.
Learn to use AI tools properly for **research**.
feel: **Anxious** about my future income, and whether I've chosen something that will shrink under me.

steps.text: Apply for a solicitor apprenticeship at a local firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and we need to be sensible. I'd say we need to protect people's work and families, and keep the country steady. I'd probably say it at chapel: look after one another, check on your neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel stuck. If AI does the thinking jobs within two years, my degree is nothing and the solicitor apprenticeship might be too. The only thing that looks stable is the farm, which is hands-on, and that's where Dad has been telling me I belong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go home more weekends and learn the farm properly: milking, the machinery, the accounts. I'd talk to Dad about whether the farm can support two of us. I'd stop buying anything I don't need and put every spare pound into savings. I'd keep studying, but not with the same hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I feel guilty for even thinking about leaving the degree, because my parents paid for it, but I can see why I'd want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you if it arrives within two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking side would change on day one: milk contracts, markets, planning. Robots would take about three more years to reach the cowshed, though. So there'd be a gap where the farm's paperwork changes but the hands-on work remains. That's where I'd be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at the farm in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to tell my parents that I'm worried about the degree. It's hard for me to do. Dad's proud I'm at university, and Mum has told everyone at the school. But I think they'd understand, because they're sensible people.

say: I'd say we need to protect people's **work** and families and keep the country steady.
I'd say at chapel: look after one another and check on your **neighbours**.

The only stable thing is the **farm**, because it's hands-on.

feel: **Anxious**, and guilty for thinking about leaving a degree my parents paid for.

fieldNote: He finds a role in the **gap** between thinking AI and hands-on robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a chance to do this properly. People should be able to retrain, and families should be able to hold on to what they've built. I'd say we need good training, sensible rules, and employers who take on young people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel more settled. I'd graduate in 2029, which gives me two working years before the big change, and I could use those to build a base. I'd probably go for a solicitor or accountancy traineeship, something with rules and a licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and start applying for traineeships in my second year. I'd learn the AI tools as they come, because I'd be using them every day in the job. I'd save about 35 a week and keep working summers on the farm, in case I need that fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not frightened. Five years is long enough to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to quit out of panic. I'd say finish the year, talk to someone who's done what he wants to do, and decide in the summer. It's a rule my dad has: never make a big decision on a bad day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend in the pub who wants to quit his course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be running for the farm. With five I can still do the degree and keep both doors open. That matters to me, because I don't want to have to choose too early.

I'd tell a friend not to quit out of **panic**.

A solicitor or accountancy **traineeship** with rules and a licence looks sensible.

Save 35 a week and keep working **summers** on the farm as a fallback.
feel: **Uneasy**, not frightened, because five years is long enough to prepare.

fieldNote: Five years lets him keep **both doors** open: degree and farm.
He quotes his father's rule about big decisions on bad days.
He now leans toward traineeships with licences, such as law or accountancy.

steps.text: Finish the degree and apply for traineeships in second year
Keep working summers on the farm as a fallback
Save 35 a week from pub wages
Use AI tools for coursework so they're familiar at work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's plenty of time, and we'd be foolish not to use it. I'd say let's build good apprenticeships, keep families strong, and let people work for what they earn. I'd talk about it on the rugby field and at church, and not worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm pretty calm. I'd be 28, qualified, perhaps married, perhaps with a kid. The big change would still be coming, but I'd have a profession and a family around me. I'd also keep an eye on the farm, because it would be a good thing to come back to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree or take the apprenticeship, qualify as a solicitor, and work near home. I'd save steadily into a pension and a house deposit. I'd use AI tools as they prove themselves, and I'd help Dad make the farm's paperwork easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the version where my plans make sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years: what does that leave you free to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to back apprenticeships and small businesses, keep taxes sensible, and help people who lose work to retrain. I don't want handouts, but I do want a fair chance. If they do that, I'd trust the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want the people running the country to do in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years lets me live my life in the right order: study, work, family. That's what I'd ask for. Not a guarantee, just a sensible timeline.

say: I'd say we'd be foolish not to use ten years to build good **apprenticeships**.
I'd talk about it on the rugby field and at **church**.
think: I'd be 28, qualified and perhaps married, with a **profession** and family around me.
The farm would be a good thing to come **back** to.
do: Qualify as a **solicitor** and work near home, close to my family.
Save steadily into a **pension** and a house deposit from my first salary.
feel: **Calm**, because in this version my plans make sense.
S4.quote: I don't want handouts, but I do want a fair chance.
fieldNote: He frames it as a **fair chance**, not handouts, in keeping with his traditional views.
Ten years lets him live things in the right order: study, work, family.
The farm stays a fallback and a place to return to.

steps.text: Qualify as a solicitor through a local apprenticeship
Save steadily into a pension and a house deposit
Help Dad make the farm's paperwork easier
Back apprenticeship schemes in local elections

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It would take my degree and the farm's paperwork and the milk contract all at once, and there'd be no time to do anything sensible. What would help is honest advice, apprenticeships for people like me, and for the government to stay out of the way where it isn't needed and step in where it is.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not sure university is the right route for me. I'm halfway between the degree and the idea of training as a solicitor on the job. I'd say, don't tell eighteen-year-olds that one path fits everyone.

headlineQuote: Don't tell eighteen-year-olds that one path fits everyone.
portrait: Ben is 18 and studies **philosophy, politics and economics**, plays rugby and pulls pints at a pub near campus.
His father is a **dairy farmer** and his mother works in a school office; they pay about half his costs.
He is traditional and favours work, apprenticeships and family support, and he uses AI tools **now and then**.
His mood runs from uneasy to anxious as time shrinks, because of the **degree** and the milk price.
He is torn between the degree and a **solicitor apprenticeship**, and he wants honest advice before he decides.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, since it hits his degree, the farm's paperwork and the milk contract at once.
whatWouldHelp: He wants honest advice, **apprenticeships** for people like him, and a government that steps in only where it must.
